The researchers think small irritations add up. If minor annoyances stop turning into bigger reactions, that may free up emotional space for better mental health overall. Patience seems to set a steady base. It just does not fix a crisis of meaning.

sections.label: The experiment
sections.text: 274 students at a large Christian university in the southern United States took surveys in their first semester and again in their final year. They rated how often they had religious or spiritual struggles in the past year, their anxiety symptoms in the past week, and their levels of the three kinds of patience. The team used a method called latent change score modeling. It separates where each student started from how they changed, so researchers can better see which changes move together over time.

sections.label: Key takeaways
items: Struggles with faith went with higher anxiety, both at the start of college and as they grew over four years.
Patience did not soften that link. Doubts that shake core beliefs may need more than staying calm.
Growing more patient with daily hassles was the one change that matched falling anxiety by the final year.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: All students came from one religious university, where faith is part of daily campus life and struggles may be easier to see. Results may differ at non-religious colleges or in the general public. Spiritual struggles were measured with a single survey question, so the study cannot tell an argument with a pastor apart from secret doubt about God. Everything was self-reported, and the authors note the statistical models are very complex for only 274 people. The study tracked links over time; it did not test whether training patience lowers anxiety. Larger, more varied studies are needed.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Patience will not answer your biggest questions, but it may stop the small things from piling up.

recall.q: Did patience protect students from the anxiety linked to spiritual struggles, and which kind of patience matched lower anxiety over four years?
recall.a: No. Patience did not soften the link between faith struggles and anxiety, probably because those struggles shake a person's core beliefs. But students who grew more patient with daily hassles had less anxiety by their final year, so patience seems to help mental health on a separate track.

cards.title: Browser fingerprinting: tracking that survives deleting cookies
cards.body: Cookies were files saved in your browser, so you could see them and delete them. Fingerprinting saves nothing. It reads your device itself, and that reading comes out the same on every visit.

sections.text:
Then: third-party cookies. Ad companies saved these small files in your browser to follow you from site to site. By 2019 they had become bad PR. Safari and Firefox already blocked them, and the EU had brought in consent banners. In 2020, Google promised to remove them from Chrome. About five years later, it kept them. Its replacement, called Privacy Sandbox, worked poorly and raised antitrust concerns, meaning worries that Google had unfair power over the market.

Now: fingerprinting. Every visit already tells the site your browser, language, operating system and IP address. The IP address often shows your location. Then the page's code checks your hardware, and it never asks your permission. It times an audio tone and reads your graphics chip. It draws text and checks the pixels. It reads your time zone, CPU core count and memory. Each trait on its own is common. Together they are almost unique to you.

sections.label: The numbers
items: Over 60% of Americans can be identified by just three traits: ZIP code, birth date and sex.
Chrome holds about two-thirds of the browser market.

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: The author says that using Chrome is like wearing an ID on your forehead. Privacy extensions can backfire: so few people use them that having one makes you easier to spot. A VPN hides the location your IP address gives away, but not your time zone. Safari and Firefox help a little. Only Brave, Tor and Mullvad Browser have strong built-in protection.

recall.q: Why can't you clear a browser fingerprint the way you could clear cookies?
recall.a: A cookie is a file saved in your browser, so you can delete it. A fingerprint saves nothing. It is built from readings of your device, like the graphics chip, time zone, CPU cores and the way it draws text. Those readings come out the same on every visit.
